title: Generating Robot Gaze on the Basis of Participation Roles and Dominance Estimation in Multiparty Interaction

fields.value: Empirical multiparty conversation studies and a human–robot interaction experiment, alongside development and evaluation of a dominance estimation and robot gaze generation system.

quotes.text: First, we conducted an empirical study and analyzed its results that showed how gaze behaviors are affected by both dominance and participation roles.

In order to examine whether the robot gaze generated by the proposed mechanism affects the user’s impression and behavior in the group communication with the robot, we conducted an evaluation experiment.

fields.value: In the evaluation, robot gaze condition had a significant effect on humans’ received gazes: gaze was more active and frequent in the dominant-robot condition than in the no-model condition (F(2, 69) = 3.641, p < 0.05). The no-model condition also showed a significant difference in utterance counts by dominance rank, with Rank 1 speaking more than Rank 3 (F(2, 23) = 4.695, p < 0.05). Dominant participants’ liking ratings correlated significantly with dominance in the less-dominant robot condition (r = 0.397, p < 0.05).

quotes.text: In the DOM and the LDOM conditions, no statistical difference was found among the three participants. On the contrary, in the NM condition, the number of utterances was different depending on dominance ranking (F(2, 23) 4.695, p<0.05).

We used two-way ANOVA in order to examine the effects of experimental conditions and dominance ranking, and found that the main effect of the experimental conditions was statistically significant (F(2, 69) 3.641, p<0.05).

These results indicate that nonverbal communication via gaze is more active and frequent in the DOM condition than the NM condition, suggesting that the robot in the DOM condition was successfully facilitating the group communication.

On the contrary, in the LDOM condition, in which the robot paid longer and more frequent attention to the dominant participants than to the other participants, the dominance score was significantly correlated with liking of the robot.

fields.value: Robot gaze behavior generation based on participation roles and conversational dominance; the authors describe gaze as an attentional behavior and nonverbal feedback signal.

quotes.text: This article has the goal of building a robot that can convey appropriate attentional behaviors according to its participation role and the dominance in human-robot multiparty conversations.
Gaze is an important nonverbal feedback signal in multiparty face-to-face conversations.
Once the participation roles and the dominance are estimated, the robot’s gaze is determined using the gaze-transition models proposed in Section 5.2.

fields.value: The paper treats gaze as feedback and as a means to coordinate multiparty communication through participation roles and dominance; gaze can direct attention to participants and facilitate turn-taking opportunities.

quotes.text: Gaze is an important nonverbal feedback signal in multiparty face-to-face conversations.

Mutlu et al. [2009] designed robot gaze behavior for three types of participant roles: addressee, bystander, and overhearer. They found that the robot’s gaze successfully regulated participation roles (called footing in their paper) in human-robot conversations, and gave the subjects feelings of groupness and liking of the robot.

Although we did not find clear results for the DOM condition in the subjective measures, in the objective measures, the robot’s gaze in this condition successfully granted more opportunities to the submissive participants to take a turn.

fields.value: Dominant participants rated the robot more positively when it behaved as less dominant and looked at them more. Robot gaze condition also affected gaze exchange: the dominant-robot condition produced more frequent human-to-human gaze than the no-model condition, while no-model gaze was associated with submissive participants having difficulty taking turns.

quotes.text: The higher the dominance score, the better the subject’s impressions of the robot.

These results indicate that nonverbal communication via gaze is more active and frequent in the DOM condition than the NM condition, suggesting that the robot in the DOM condition was successfully facilitating the group communication.

This might have occurred because the gaze exchange between the subjects was less frequent in the NM condition, and submissive participants had less opportunity to receive the others’ attention to start a turn compared with the DOM condition.

fields.value: The system estimates dominance with a regression model using gaze-at-others, mutual gaze, speech amount, and silence-breaking measures. Kinect face tracking estimates head direction; a Microcone microphone array provides speaker direction and speech signals. Participation roles are assigned using speaker diarization, gaze-based addressee identification, and identification of remaining people as side participants. Robot gaze transitions follow role- and dominance-based models; speech responses in the interaction were Wizard-of-Oz controlled.

quotes.text: As a result, four independent variables were selected: amount of gaze at others, amount of mutual gaze, amount of speech, and breaking a silence.

We use the Kinect face tracking functionality to recognize the head direction of the participants because this device is much easier to set up than a motion-capture system and markers are not necessary.
The audio-source angle is obtained by a microcone that can recognize six different directions using a microphone array. The system identifies the speaker from the audio-source angle.

As with the previous experiment, the robot’s verbal response was determined manually using a WOZ system; however, in this experiment, the robot’s gaze was automatically generated using our gaze generation mechanism.

fields.value: The authors state that physical robot systems avoid the Mona Lisa gaze effect associated with two-dimensional projected characters, making the dominance model potentially more useful; the evaluation uses head direction to express gaze.

quotes.text: In our dominance estimation model, gaze direction approximated based on head direction is an important predictor. Thus, our model may be more useful for physical robot systems, in which the Mona Liza gaze effect can be avoided.
The head gaze is maintained for the time period provided by the model.

fields.value: The paper developed a system that estimates conversational dominance and uses it with participation roles to generate a humanoid robot’s gaze during group conversations. In evaluation, dominant participants liked the robot more when it behaved as less dominant and attended to them, while the dominant-gaze condition increased human-to-human gaze compared with simply looking at the current speaker.

RQ1; RQ2; RQ3; RQ4; RQ5; RQ6 — The paper frames gaze as nonverbal feedback and attention behavior, analyzes its role in multiparty coordination, and measures effects on impressions, gaze exchange, and turn-taking. It details sensing and gaze generation, uses a Robovie R3 humanoid, and discusses how physical embodiment avoids the Mona Lisa gaze effect.
